blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Understanding foundational concepts provides the essential framework for advanced exam preparation.
Core definitions and basic terminology serve as building blocks for complex analytical questions.
Introductory overviews help map out the scope and structure of the entire subject syllabus.

blocks.content: The number system is the foundation of all mathematical calculations. In competitive exams like  CGL, CHSL, and SI, questions on number systems appear regularly. Understanding the classification, properties, and operations on numbers is essential.

cells: Sum of first n natural numbers = n(n+1)/2
Sum of first n odd numbers = n²
Sum of first n even numbers = n(n+1)
Sum of squares of first n natural numbers = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6
Sum of cubes of first n natural numbers = [n(n+1)/2]²

Example 1: Find the sum of all natural numbers from 1 to 100.

Solution: Sum = n(n+1)/2 = 100×101/2 = 5050

Example 2: What is the sum of the first 20 odd numbers?

Solution: Sum of first n odd numbers = n² = 20² = 400

Example 3: Which of these is NOT a prime: 97, 91, 83, 79?

Solution: 91 = 7 × 13, so 91 is NOT prime. Others are prime.

Example 4: Find the number of primes between 50 and 70.

Solution: Primes: 53, 59, 61, 67 → 4 prime numbers

Example 5: Is 4862 divisible by 4?

Solution: Last two digits = 62. 62 ÷ 4 = 15.5 → NOT divisible by 4
For exams, memorise divisibility rules for 2 through 13. Note: 1 is NEITHER prime NOR composite. 2 is the ONLY even prime number.

blocks.content: LCM (Lowest Common Multiple) and HCF (Highest Common Factor) are two of the most frequently tested topics in  and SI exams. Mastering these is essential for solving time, work, and remainder problems.

cells: HCF × LCM = Product of two numbers (a × b)
LCM of fractions = LCM of numerators / HCF of denominators
HCF of fractions = HCF of numerators / LCM of denominators

blocks.content: 2.3 Methods to Find LCM and HCF

cells: Divide by common primes until all reach 1

Example 1: Find LCM and HCF of 24 and 36.

Solution: 24 = 2³×3; 36 = 2²×3². HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2³×3² = 72. Check: 12×72 = 864 = 24×36 ✓

Example 2: LCM = 180, HCF = 12, one number = 36. Find the other.

Solution: Other = (LCM × HCF) / First = (180 × 12) / 36 = 60

Example 3: Three bells toll at intervals of 6, 8 and 12 minutes. When do they toll together?

Solution: LCM(6, 8, 12) = 24 minutes
Trick: When a number leaves same remainder r with divisors a, b, c → answer is LCM(a,b,c) + r, or HCF of differences of pairs.

blocks.content: Percentage means "per hundred." It appears in almost every competitive exam — in direct questions, data interpretation, profit/loss, and interest problems.

cells: If A is x% more than B → B is [x/(100+x)] × 100% less than A
Net change for two successive % changes a and b: a + b + ab/100

Example 2: A number increased by 20% then decreased by 20%. Net change?

Solution: Net change = 20+(−20)+(20×−20)/100 = −4 → 4% decrease

Example 4: A is 25% more than B. By what % is B less than A?

Solution: B less than A = [25/(100+25)] × 100 = 20%
Always calculate % on the BASE (original) value, not the new value, unless specified otherwise.
If two items sold at same SP, one at x% profit and other at x% loss → LOSS = x²/100 %

Example 1: A shopkeeper buys goods for ₹800 and sells at 25% profit. Find SP.

Solution: SP = 800 × 125/100 = ₹1,000

Example 2: A trader sells a TV for ₹15,000 at 20% loss. Find the CP.

Solution: CP = 15000 × 100/80 = ₹18,750

Example 3: A book has MP = ₹500, discount = 15%. Find SP.

Solution: SP = 500 × 85/100 = ₹425

Example 4: Two articles sold for ₹1,200 each, one at 20% profit and other at 20% loss.

Solution: Loss % = 20²/100 = 4%. Net result: 4% loss

Example 5: A shopkeeper marks goods 40% above CP and gives 20% discount.

Solution: CP=100, MP=140, SP=140×0.8=112. Profit = 12%

Example 1: SI on ₹5,000 at 8% per annum for 3 years.

Solution: SI = 5000×8×3/100 = ₹1,200. Amount = ₹6,200

Example 2: Find CI on ₹10,000 at 10% for 2 years.

Solution: A = 10000×(1.1)² = ₹12,100. CI = ₹2,100

Example 3: Difference between CI and SI on ₹8,000 at 5% for 2 years.

Solution: Difference = P×(R/100)² = 8000×0.0025 = ₹20

Example 4: A sum triples itself in 10 years under SI. Find the rate.

Solution: SI = 2P. R = (2P×100)/(P×10) = 20% p.a.
CI is always greater than SI for same P, R, T (when T > 1 year). The difference grows rapidly with time.
Train crosses a platform: t = (Length of Train + Length of Platform) / Speed

Example 1: A car travels 120 km in 2 hours. Find speed in km/h and m/s.

Solution: Speed = 60 km/h = 60×5/18 ≈ 16.67 m/s

Example 2: A man walks at 5 km/h and returns at 3 km/h. Average speed?

Solution: Avg = 2×5×3/(5+3) = 30/8 = 3.75 km/h

Example 3: A 200m train crosses a 300m bridge at 50 m/s. Find time.

Solution: Time = (200+300)/50 = 10 seconds

Example 4: Two trains 150m and 200m long run at 60 and 90 km/h opposite directions.

Solution: Relative speed = 150 km/h = 125/3 m/s. Time = 350/(125/3) = 8.4 s
Sum of all angles of a triangle = 180°
Exterior angle = Sum of two non-adjacent interior angles

Example 1: Two angles of a triangle are 65° and 75°. Find the third.

Solution: 180° − 65° − 75° = 40°

Example 2: Find the area of a triangle with sides 3, 4, 5.

Solution: s=6. Area = √(6×3×2×1) = 6 sq. units

Example 3: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. Find hypotenuse.

Solution: h = √(25+144) = √169 = 13

Example 4: Exterior angle is 120°. One interior angle is 70°. Find the other remote angle.

Solution: Remote = 120° − 70° = 50°
sin θ = Opposite/Hypotenuse | cos θ = Adjacent/Hypotenuse | tan θ = sin/cos

Example 2: If sin θ = 3/5, find cos θ and tan θ.

Solution: cos θ = 4/5, tan θ = 3/4 (Pythagorean triple 3,4,5)

Example 3: A tower 100m tall casts a shadow 100/√3 m. Find angle of elevation.

Solution: tan θ = 100/(100/√3) = √3 → θ = 60°

Example 4: If tanθ + cotθ = 2, find sin θ.

Solution: tan²θ−2tanθ+1=0 → tanθ=1 → θ=45° → sinθ=1/√2

blocks.content: Understanding which topics carry the most weightage helps you prioritise your preparation. The pie chart below shows typical  exam topic distribution:

cells:
Example 1: If total marks = 1000, how many from Arithmetic?

Solution: 30% of 1000 = 300 marks

Example 2: What is the ratio of Geometry to Data Interpretation marks?

Solution: 15:12 = 5:4

Example 3: Geometry and Mensuration together form what % of total?

Solution: 15 + 13 = 28%

Example 4: In 2022, by how much did City A outperform City B?

Solution: City A=70, City B=58. Difference = 12 marks
In DI, first read the chart title, legend, and units carefully. Never rush into calculation — understand what each axis/segment represents.
